questions.question: What are the ACID properties of a database transaction?
questions.title: ACID Properties of Database Transactions
questions.direct_answer: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability — the four properties that guarantee database transactions are processed reliably. Atomicity ensures all-or-nothing execution, Consistency maintains database rules, Isolation prevents concurrent transaction interference, and Durability guarantees committed data survives system failures.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand what each ACID property means in practice and can explain why each matters with concrete examples.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Memorizing the four-letter acronym without understanding scenarios where each property prevents data corruption or loss.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use the bank transfer example to illustrate all four properties simultaneously, showing how removing any one property breaks data integrity.

sections.title: Why ACID Properties Matter for Database Reliability
sections.content: ACID properties are the foundation of **transactional databases** like PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Oracle. They guarantee that your data stays correct even when multiple users access it simultaneously or when the server crashes mid-operation. Think of a bank transfer: when you send $100 from Account A to Account B, the database must subtract from A and add to B as one indivisible unit — not half-complete if the power goes out. **Atomicity** makes operations all-or-nothing, **Consistency** enforces your business rules (like no negative balances), **Isolation** prevents two transfers from interfering with each other, and **Durability** ensures completed transfers survive crashes. Without these four properties working together, you'd lose money, see phantom balances, or corrupt your entire ledger. Modern applications rely on ACID to handle payments, inventory updates, user registrations — any operation where partial completion is unacceptable.

sections.title: ACID in Action: Bank Transfer with Spring @Transactional
Key Points
content: **Atomicity**: All operations in a transaction succeed together or fail together — no partial updates. If any step fails, the database rolls back all changes as if nothing happened.
**Consistency**: Transactions move the database from one valid state to another, enforcing all constraints (foreign keys, unique indexes, check constraints) throughout the operation.
**Isolation**: Concurrent transactions don't see each other's intermediate states. PostgreSQL's default isolation level (Read Committed) prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads.
**Durability**: Once a transaction commits, the changes are permanent — even if the server crashes one second later. The database writes to persistent storage (disk) before confirming the commit.
**@Transactional in Spring**: Automatically applies ACID by starting a transaction, executing the method, and committing on success or rolling back on unchecked exceptions.
**Real-world impact**: Without ACID, double-spending bugs occur — a user could withdraw the same $100 twice if two requests hit the server simultaneously.
**Trade-off**: Strong ACID guarantees reduce throughput — databases lock rows or use MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) to maintain isolation, which limits parallelism.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability — four properties that keep database transactions reliable. Let me explain each with a bank transfer example. Atomicity means the operation is all-or-nothing. If I'm transferring a hundred dollars from Account A to Account B, the database subtracts from A and adds to B as one unit. If the server crashes halfway through, the entire operation rolls back — you never see just the withdrawal without the deposit. Consistency enforces business rules. The database won't let Account A go negative if you've got a check constraint for that. It validates every constraint before committing. Isolation prevents interference between concurrent transactions. If two users transfer money at the same time, they don't see each other's half-done work. PostgreSQL uses MVCC to give each transaction a consistent snapshot of the data. Durability guarantees that once the database says commit succeeded, that data survives a crash. It's written to disk before the commit returns. In Spring Boot, we use the at-Transactional annotation to get all four properties automatically. If an exception is thrown inside that method, Spring rolls back the transaction — that's atomicity in action. One mistake freshers make is thinking ACID is just theory. It's not. Without it, you'd have double-spending bugs where two requests withdraw the same money because they both read the balance before either one updates it. That's why every payment system relies on ACID databases.

questions.question: How does Spring's @Transactional annotation work?
questions.title: How @Transactional Works in Spring
questions.direct_answer: The at-Transactional annotation tells Spring to wrap a method in a database transaction, automatically starting the transaction before the method executes and committing on success or rolling back if an unchecked exception is thrown. Spring uses AOP proxies to intercept method calls and inject transaction management code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Spring knowledge — at-Transactional is used in almost every Spring Data application, so you must understand its behavior.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking at-Transactional works when called from within the same class — Spring's AOP proxy doesn't intercept self-invocation, so the transaction never starts.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the self-invocation caveat and explain that at-Transactional on private methods also doesn't work — only public methods on Spring beans are proxied.

sections.title: How Spring Manages Transactions with AOP Proxies
sections.content: The **at-Transactional** annotation is Spring's declarative way to manage database transactions without writing boilerplate code. When you mark a method with at-Transactional, Spring creates an **AOP proxy** around your bean — a wrapper object that intercepts method calls. Before the real method runs, the proxy starts a database transaction. After the method completes successfully, the proxy commits the transaction. If an **unchecked exception** (RuntimeException or Error) is thrown, the proxy rolls back the transaction to undo all changes. This keeps your business logic clean: you write straightforward Java methods, and Spring handles the begin-commit-rollback lifecycle. The proxy approach is why at-Transactional only works on public methods of Spring-managed beans — Spring can't intercept private methods or calls from within the same class (self-invocation). Understanding this proxy mechanism is crucial because many production bugs in Spring apps come from misusing at-Transactional in scenarios where the proxy isn't invoked.

sections.title: Correct and Incorrect @Transactional Usage
Key Points
content: **AOP proxy pattern**: Spring wraps your bean in a proxy object that adds transaction logic before and after method calls. The proxy calls entityManager.getTransaction().begin() before your code runs.
**Rollback behavior**: By default, at-Transactional rolls back only on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and Error). Checked exceptions cause a commit unless you specify rollbackFor.

**Self-invocation trap**: Calling this.methodWithTransactional() from within the same class bypasses the proxy — no transaction starts. Always call transactional methods through injected dependencies.
**Private methods ignored**: Spring's AOP can't proxy private methods, so at-Transactional on private methods silently does nothing. Only public methods on Spring beans are intercepted.
**Propagation levels**: REQUIRED (default) joins existing transaction or starts new one. REQUIRES_NEW always starts a fresh transaction, suspending the current one.
**Read-only optimization**: at-Transactional(readOnly = true) tells the database this transaction won't modify data, allowing optimizations like skipping dirty checks.

**Transaction boundaries**: A transaction spans the entire method execution, including all repository calls and service calls. Lazy-loaded collections must be accessed inside the transaction or you'll get LazyInitializationException.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The at-Transactional annotation tells Spring to automatically manage database transactions for a method. When you call that method, Spring doesn't invoke it directly — it goes through an AOP proxy that Spring created. That proxy starts a transaction before your method runs, and then commits the transaction if the method succeeds. If an unchecked exception is thrown, the proxy rolls back instead. This way you don't write begin-commit-rollback code yourself. Now here's the critical part that trips up a lot of developers. The proxy only intercepts calls that come from outside the class. If you call a transactional method from another method in the same class — we call that self-invocation — Spring's proxy isn't in the call path, so no transaction starts. I've seen production bugs where someone marked a helper method with at-Transactional and called it with this-dot-method-name, and the transaction never happened. Same issue with private methods — Spring can't proxy them, so at-Transactional silently does nothing. You have to make it public and call it through an injected bean reference. One more thing: by default, only unchecked exceptions trigger rollback. If you throw a checked exception, Spring commits the transaction. If you want checked exceptions to roll back too, you specify rollbackFor equals Exception dot class. Understanding this proxy mechanism is essential because it explains why at-Transactional behaves differently depending on where you call the method from.

questions.question: What are the four database transaction isolation levels and what read anomalies do they prevent?
questions.title: Transaction Isolation Levels Explained
questions.direct_answer: The four isolation levels are READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE. Each prevents progressively more read anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads. Higher isolation means better consistency but lower concurrency and performance.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the trade-off between consistency and performance in concurrent database access and can explain what anomalies each level prevents.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking SERIALIZABLE is always best — it prevents all anomalies but serializes concurrent transactions, severely hurting throughput.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Know that MySQL's default is REPEATABLE READ and PostgreSQL's default is READ COMMITTED — and be able to say which anomalies each prevents with examples.

sections.title: Why Isolation Levels Matter in Concurrent Systems
sections.content: **Transaction isolation levels** control how concurrent transactions interact with each other. When multiple users or services access the database simultaneously, isolation determines what data each transaction can see. The challenge is balancing **consistency** against **performance**. Stricter isolation gives you more predictable data but requires the database to lock more aggressively, which slows down concurrent operations. Looser isolation allows better concurrency but risks **read anomalies** — situations where a transaction reads incorrect or inconsistent data because of another concurrent transaction. There are three main anomalies: **dirty reads** (reading uncommitted changes that get rolled back), **non-repeatable reads** (same query returns different results within one transaction), and **phantom reads** (new rows appear in range queries). The four standard isolation levels each prevent a different subset of these anomalies. PostgreSQL defaults to READ COMMITTED, MySQL to REPEATABLE READ — understanding these defaults matters because your application behavior depends on them.

sections.title: Step 1: READ UNCOMMITTED — No Isolation
sections.content: READ UNCOMMITTED is the lowest isolation level. A transaction can read data that another transaction has modified but not yet committed — called a **dirty read**. If the other transaction rolls back, your transaction just read data that never officially existed. This is almost never used in production because the data integrity risk is too high. Imagine reading an account balance that includes a pending debit, then making a decision based on that balance, only to have the debit rolled back. You made a decision on phantom data. The only advantage is maximum concurrency — no read locks at all. PostgreSQL doesn't even support this level; it treats it as READ COMMITTED.

sections.title: Step 2: READ COMMITTED — Prevents Dirty Reads
sections.content: READ COMMITTED ensures you only read data that has been committed. It prevents dirty reads but allows **non-repeatable reads** and **phantom reads**. If you query the same row twice in one transaction, you might get different results if another transaction commits a change between your two queries. This is PostgreSQL's default and appropriate for most web applications. Example: you query a product's stock level, see 10 units, then query it again a second later and see 8 units because another transaction committed a purchase. For most use cases, this is acceptable. The performance is good because read locks are released immediately after each statement, not held for the entire transaction.

sections.title: Step 3: REPEATABLE READ — Prevents Non-Repeatable Reads
sections.content: REPEATABLE READ ensures that if you read a row at the start of a transaction, reading it again gives you the same values even if other transactions commit changes. It prevents dirty reads and non-repeatable reads but still allows **phantom reads** — new rows appearing in range queries. MySQL's default level is REPEATABLE READ. It uses multi-version concurrency control so readers don't block writers. However, in MySQL, InnoDB actually prevents phantom reads too using gap locks, so it's effectively stronger than the SQL standard requires. Use this level when you need snapshot consistency across multiple queries — like generating a financial report where all numbers must be from the same point in time.

sections.title: Step 4: SERIALIZABLE — Full Isolation
sections.content: SERIALIZABLE is the highest isolation level. Transactions execute as if they ran one at a time with zero concurrency. It prevents all three anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads. The database achieves this by locking ranges of rows or by detecting conflicts and rolling back one transaction. The cost is severe performance degradation under high concurrency — transactions effectively queue up waiting for locks. Use SERIALIZABLE only when absolute consistency is critical and concurrency is low, like processing end-of-day batch financial reconciliations. For typical web applications with hundreds of concurrent requests, SERIALIZABLE would create a bottleneck. Most production systems use READ COMMITTED or REPEATABLE READ.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Dirty read**: reading uncommitted data that might be rolled back. Only READ UNCOMMITTED allows this; all other levels prevent it.

**Non-repeatable read**: reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values because another transaction committed an update. READ COMMITTED allows this; higher levels prevent it.

**Phantom read**: a range query returns different rows on subsequent executions because another transaction inserted or deleted rows. READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ allow this; SERIALIZABLE prevents it.
**PostgreSQL default**: READ COMMITTED. Good balance for web applications with high concurrency and acceptable eventual consistency.
**MySQL default**: REPEATABLE READ. InnoDB's implementation actually prevents phantom reads too, making it stricter than the SQL standard.
**Performance trade-off**: stricter isolation requires more locking or conflict detection, which reduces throughput. Most systems use READ COMMITTED or REPEATABLE READ, not SERIALIZABLE.
**Setting isolation in Spring**: use the isolation attribute on at-Transactional, like at-Transactional with isolation equals Isolation dot REPEATABLE underscore READ.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: There are four transaction isolation levels that control what data a transaction can see when other transactions are running concurrently. They're ordered from weakest to strongest isolation. READ UNCOMMITTED is the lowest level. It allows dirty reads, meaning you can read data that another transaction modified but hasn't committed yet. If that transaction rolls back, you just read data that never officially existed. This is almost never used in production. READ COMMITTED is the next level and it's PostgreSQL's default. It prevents dirty reads — you only see committed data. But it allows non-repeatable reads, meaning if you query the same row twice in your transaction, you might get different values if another transaction commits a change in between. For most web apps, this is totally fine. REPEATABLE READ is stronger. Once you read a row, you'll get the same values every time you read it again in that transaction, even if other transactions commit updates. MySQL defaults to this level. It prevents dirty reads and non-repeatable reads, but it still allows phantom reads — new rows appearing in range queries. SERIALIZABLE is the strictest level. It prevents all three anomalies by making transactions execute as if they ran one at a time with no concurrency. The catch is performance — under high load, transactions essentially queue up waiting for locks, which kills throughput. The key trade-off is consistency versus concurrency. Stricter isolation gives you more predictable data but reduces how many transactions can run simultaneously. Most production systems use READ COMMITTED or REPEATABLE READ. You'd only use SERIALIZABLE for critical operations like financial reconciliations where perfect consistency matters more than speed.

questions.question: What is transaction propagation in Spring and what is the difference between REQUIRED and REQUIRES_NEW?
questions.title: Spring Transaction Propagation: REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW
questions.direct_answer: Transaction propagation defines how a transactional method behaves when called from within another transaction. REQUIRED, the default, joins the existing transaction if one is active or starts a new one if not. REQUIRES_NEW always suspends the current transaction and starts a completely independent new transaction.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of transaction propagation — shows you know that at-Transactional has behavior beyond just wrapping a method in begin/commit/rollback.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that REQUIRED is the default, or thinking every at-Transactional always creates a new transaction regardless of context.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a use case for REQUIRES_NEW: audit logging that should be committed even if the main transaction rolls back, or processing individual batch items independently.

sections.title: What Transaction Propagation Controls
sections.content: **Transaction propagation** determines what happens when a transactional method calls another transactional method. Should they share the same transaction or run in separate ones? This matters because transactions are expensive — starting and committing them involves coordination with the database — but you also need control over transaction boundaries. Spring defines seven propagation behaviors, but **REQUIRED** and **REQUIRES_NEW** are the most common. REQUIRED, the default, means the method participates in the calling transaction if one exists. If your controller calls a service method and both are marked transactional with REQUIRED, only one transaction is created — they share it. If the service method fails and rolls back, the entire transaction including the controller's work rolls back too. REQUIRES_NEW is different: it **suspends** the current transaction, starts a brand new one, and commits or rolls back that new transaction independently. This is useful when you need part of an operation to be permanent even if the rest fails — like audit logging or processing batch items where one failure shouldn't stop the others.

sections.title: When to Use Each Propagation Type
sections.content: Use **REQUIRED** for 99 percent of your transactional methods. It's the default for a reason — most business operations should succeed or fail together as a single unit. If you're processing an order, the inventory reduction, payment processing, and order record creation should all be part of one transaction. If payment fails, you want inventory and the order record rolled back too. Use **REQUIRES_NEW** when you need transactional independence within a larger operation. The classic example is **audit logging**: you want to record that a user attempted an operation even if the operation itself fails and rolls back. Wrap your audit save in a REQUIRES_NEW method so its commit happens separately. Another use case is **batch processing**: when processing a list of items, you might want each item in its own transaction so one failure doesn't stop the entire batch. Mark your process-single-item method as REQUIRES_NEW. The caveat is that REQUIRES_NEW is expensive — suspending and resuming transactions has overhead — so don't overuse it.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **REQUIRED**: joins the current transaction if one exists, otherwise starts a new one. This is the default propagation and appropriate for most methods.
**REQUIRES_NEW**: always starts a new transaction, suspending the current one if it exists. The new transaction commits or rolls back independently.
**Rollback behavior with REQUIRED**: if the inner method fails, the entire outer transaction is marked for rollback. All work done in both methods is rolled back together.
**Rollback behavior with REQUIRES_NEW**: if the inner method fails, only its transaction rolls back. The outer transaction can still commit successfully.
**Audit logging use case**: save audit records with REQUIRES_NEW so they're committed even if the main operation fails. You want evidence of the attempt regardless of outcome.
**Batch processing use case**: process each item in REQUIRES_NEW so one item's failure doesn't prevent others from succeeding. Each item gets its own independent transaction.
**Other propagation types**: SUPPORTS runs in a transaction if one exists but doesn't start one; MANDATORY requires an existing transaction or throws exception; NEVER fails if a transaction exists.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Transaction propagation controls what happens when you call a transactional method from inside another transaction. The two most important types are REQUIRED and REQUIRES_NEW. REQUIRED is the default propagation. It means if a transaction already exists, the method joins it. If no transaction exists, it starts a new one. So if your controller calls a service method and both have at-Transactional, they share one transaction. If the service method throws an exception, the entire transaction rolls back, including any work the controller did before calling the service. This is what you want for most business logic — operations that should succeed or fail together. REQUIRES_NEW is different. It always starts a new transaction, even if one already exists. It suspends the current transaction, runs your method in a brand new transaction, commits or rolls back that transaction, and then resumes the outer one. The inner transaction is completely independent. If it fails and rolls back, the outer transaction can still succeed. The classic use case for REQUIRES_NEW is audit logging. You want to record that a user attempted an operation even if the operation fails. Wrap your audit save call in a REQUIRES_NEW method, and it'll be committed to the database regardless of whether the main operation succeeds or rolls back. Another example is batch processing. If you're processing a hundred orders, you might want each order in its own transaction so one failure doesn't stop the other ninety-nine. The trade-off is performance — suspending and resuming transactions has overhead, so don't overuse REQUIRES_NEW. Stick with REQUIRED for normal business logic.

questions.question: In practice, when do you actually need a database transaction?
questions.title: When Do You Need a Database Transaction?
questions.direct_answer: You need a database transaction whenever two or more operations must succeed or fail together to maintain data consistency. Any multi-step operation where a partial update would leave your data in an inconsistent state requires a transaction. Single operations that don't depend on other operations typically don't need explicit transactions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical judgment — knowing when to use transactions versus when a single operation doesn't need explicit transaction management.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Wrapping every single database call in at-Transactional even when there's only one operation — unnecessary overhead and code clutter.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name specific real-world scenarios: order creation with inventory updates, money transfers, user registration with email verification records — and explain why each requires a transaction.

sections.title: The Core Rule for When You Need Transactions
sections.content: The fundamental question is: **can my data be left in an inconsistent state if this operation partially completes?** If the answer is yes, you need a transaction. Transactions guarantee atomicity — all operations complete together or none do. Think about creating an order in an e-commerce system. You need to save the order record, reduce inventory for each item, and maybe charge the customer's payment method. If you save the order but the inventory update fails, you've oversold your stock. If inventory is reduced but the order isn't saved, you've lost items with no record of the sale. Both scenarios break data consistency, so you wrap all three operations in one transaction. Conversely, a **single database operation doesn't need explicit transaction management**. When you call save on a repository for one entity, the ORM (Hibernate/JPA) wraps it in a transaction automatically. Adding at-Transactional around a single save is redundant. The key is recognizing **multi-step business operations** that modify multiple entities or tables.

sections.title: Step 1: Identify Multi-Entity Updates
sections.content: Ask yourself: does this operation modify more than one entity or database table? If yes, you likely need a transaction. Example: transferring money between bank accounts modifies two Account entities. Creating an order typically modifies Order, OrderItem, and Inventory entities. Registering a user might create a User entity and a UserVerification entity. All of these are multi-entity updates that should be atomic. If any one piece fails, you need to roll back all the pieces. The classic sign you need a transaction is when you have multiple save calls or a save plus an update call in one method. Without a transaction, the first save might succeed and commit while the second one fails, leaving you with partial data.

sections.title: Step 2: Consider Business Consistency Rules
sections.content: Even if you're modifying a single entity, you might need a transaction if business rules require consistency with other operations. Example: updating an order status to SHIPPED should also create a ShipmentTracking record. Those are two separate entities, and they must be kept in sync. Another case is **read-then-write operations** where the write depends on the read. If you read an account balance, calculate interest, and update the balance, you need a transaction to ensure the balance doesn't change between your read and write. Without transaction isolation, another concurrent transaction could modify the balance after you read it but before you write the new value, causing your calculation to be wrong. This is a consistency rule that requires transactional protection even though it's technically a single update.

sections.title: Step 3: Evaluate Single-Operation Scenarios
sections.content: For single database operations — one save, one update, one delete — you usually don't need to explicitly add at-Transactional. Spring Data repositories and JPA already wrap individual operations in transactions by default. Example: calling userRepository dot save on a single User entity is already transactional. Adding at-Transactional is redundant and adds proxy overhead. However, there are exceptions. If you're doing a **read-only query** but you need consistent results across multiple queries in one request, wrap them in a read-only transaction using at-Transactional with readOnly equals true. This ensures you're reading from a consistent snapshot of the database. Another exception is **bulk operations** like batch deletes or updates. Even though it's one repository call, if the operation spans many rows, you want it wrapped in a transaction so a failure mid-operation doesn't leave half the rows modified.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Multi-step operations**: if your method calls save or update on two or more entities, you need a transaction to ensure atomicity. Partial completion breaks data consistency.
**Order creation example**: saving Order, updating Inventory, and recording Payment must all succeed together. If payment fails, you must roll back the order and inventory changes.
**Money transfer example**: debiting one account and crediting another are two operations that must be atomic. Without a transaction, money could disappear or be duplicated.
**Single operations don't need explicit transactions**: one repository save call is already wrapped in a transaction by Spring Data. Adding at-Transactional is redundant.
**Read-then-write operations**: if you read data, calculate something, and write it back, you need a transaction to prevent concurrent updates from invalidating your calculation.
**Read-only transactions**: wrap multiple queries in at-Transactional with readOnly equals true to ensure you're reading from a consistent snapshot, which matters for reports.
**Batch processing caveat**: wrapping a large batch in one transaction risks long locks and rollback overhead. Consider smaller transaction scopes or REQUIRES_NEW per item.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You need a database transaction whenever two or more operations must succeed or fail together to keep your data consistent. The core question is: if this operation partially completes, will my data be in a broken state? If yes, you need a transaction. Let me give you three concrete examples. First, creating an order in an e-commerce app. You save the Order record, reduce the inventory for each product, and maybe charge the customer's payment method. If the order is saved but inventory isn't reduced, you've oversold your stock. If inventory is reduced but the order isn't saved, you've lost products with no record. So you wrap all three operations in one transaction. If any step fails, everything rolls back. Second, transferring money between bank accounts. You debit Account A and credit Account B. Those two updates must be atomic. Without a transaction, the debit could succeed but the credit fails, and money just vanishes. Or the credit succeeds but the debit fails, and you've created money out of thin air. Third, user registration. You create a User entity and a UserVerification entity that holds the email verification token. If the user is saved but verification isn't, you can't send the verification email. Both must succeed together. Now, when don't you need a transaction? Single operations don't require explicit at-Transactional. If you're calling save on one repository for one entity, Spring Data already wraps it in a transaction automatically. Adding at-Transactional is redundant. One exception is read-only queries. If you're running multiple queries to generate a report, wrap them in a read-only transaction so you're reading from a consistent snapshot. Otherwise, data could change between queries and your report numbers won't add up.

beats.text: You're deciding which service methods need @Transactional. Wrapping everything is wasteful — transactions have overhead. Only operations where partial completion corrupts data need them.

items: Definitely need a transaction: publish post + update post_count (two writes that must succeed together)
Definitely need a transaction: user registration + default settings insert (partial creates broken accounts)
Don't need a transaction: single SELECT query, single INSERT with no side effects
Maybe need a transaction: depends on business rules — inserting a comment might or might not also update a count

beats.text: Put @Transactional on service methods that call multiple repository operations. Keep it off single-read methods. Spring Data JPA repositories are already transactional for individual calls — @Transactional on the service spans multiple calls into one unit.
